title: Findings on the Rear Pressure Bulkhead of High-Cycle ZEPHYR-24 Aircraft — Request for a Design Reinforcement
abstract: High-cycle ZEPHYR-24 operator reports repeated indications on the outer segments of the rear pressure bulkhead and asks for a design reinforcement instead of the current inspection-and-repair regime, which is costing an eight-day check extension each time.

sections.request: We fly our ZEPHYR-24s on very short sectors, so they build cycles fast — two of them passed 42000 flights last year on airframes that are not yet twenty years old. At the last two heavy checks the NDT team found indications on the outer part of the rear pressure wall, near where the tailplane structure comes in, and both times the aircraft was stuck for eight extra days while an engineering repair was agreed. The area is awkward to reach, we have to strip the rear galley and the aft cargo lining to get to it, and the inspection itself takes three shifts. We would like Aeralis to give us a reinforcement we can install once, so that we can go back to the standard inspection interval instead of the reduced one we are now on.
sections.background: Two findings in eighteen months on two different aircraft, both on the outer radial segments and both starting at a fastener row. Our maintenance provider believes the cycle rate is the driver rather than any manufacturing issue, and the fleet-wide indication rate on this zone is 1.9 per 1000 flight cycles against a published expectation of 0.2. We have also had two secondary findings on the tailplane attachment area during the same access, which suggests the two should be treated together.
sections.expected_outcome: A reinforcement that restores the original inspection threshold and interval, that can be installed during a scheduled heavy check with the aft cabin already stripped, and that is compatible with the tailplane attachment work we expect to carry out in the same visit. We would accept a weight penalty of up to fifteen kilograms.

type_data.business_justification: Two unplanned check extensions of eight days each, plus a halved inspection interval applied to nine aircraft, against a sub-fleet that the operator plans to run for a further twelve years.
